claim: Prevalence for comorbid conditions of stroke ranges from 43% to 94%.

claim: Mortality in stroke, its subtypes, and their comorbid conditions have a strong ethnic bias.

evidence: The claim cites three studies (Tarko et al., 2022; Gardener et al., 2020; Mkoma et al., 2020) supporting the ethnic bias in mortality.

claim: A Danish study reported 15% higher mortality risk in presence of diabetes mellitus with end-organ damage for stroke patients.

evidence: The claim cites Schmidt et al., 2014 as the source for this mortality risk estimate.

claim: Globally, stroke ranks as the second most fatal disease in 2019 with an age-standardized mortality rate of 84.2/100,000 (95%UI 76.8–90.2).

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Ischemic heart disease is the most fatal disease globally in 2019 with an age-standardized mortality rate of 117.9/100,000 (95%UI 107.8–125.9).

claim: High systolic blood pressure ranks as the most fatal comorbid disease condition with an age-standardized mortality rate of 138.9/100,000 [95%UI 121.3–155.7] in 2019.

evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ischemic stroke ranks highest globally among stroke subtypes with an age-standardized mortality rate of 43.5/100,000 [95%UI 39.08–46.8] in 2019.

evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intracerebral hemorrhage has an age-standardized mortality rate of 36.0/100,000 [95%UI 32.9–38.7] globally in 2019.

evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Subarachnoid hemorrhage has an age-standardized mortality rate of 4.7/100,000 [95%UI 4.1–5.2] globally in 2019.

evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: High body mass index improved its rank in 2014 by swapping with high low-density lipoprotein cholesterol in age-standardized mortality rates.
source: The ranking of the ASMRs of the diseases follows the same trend throughout the last decade with minor exceptions, where high body mass index (high BMI) improved its rank in 2014 by swapping with high low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (high LDL), and type 1 diabetes (T1D) dethroned chronic kidney disease (CKD) in 2019.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal trend analysis of mortality data.

claim: Type 1 diabetes dethroned chronic kidney disease in age-standardized mortality rate ranking in 2019.
source: The ranking of the ASMRs of the diseases follows the same trend throughout the last decade with minor exceptions, where high body mass index (high BMI) improved its rank in 2014 by swapping with high low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (high LDL), and type 1 diabetes (T1D) dethroned chronic kidney disease (CKD) in 2019.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal trend analysis of mortality data.

claim: Crude incidence rates of stroke and its subtypes increased in the last decade.
source: Crude incidence rates of stroke and its subtypes increased in the last decade but ASIRs decreased, with exception of ischemic stroke, where an increase in ASIR was observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by incidence rate trend analysis.

claim: Age-standardized incidence rates of stroke and its subtypes decreased in the last decade, with exception of ischemic stroke.

claim: Ischemic stroke showed an increase in age-standardized incidence rate in the last decade.

claim: Type 2 diabetes surpassed ischemic heart disease in crude incidence rates in 2019, with T2D at 280.1/100,000 (95%UI 258.8–303.9) and IHD at 274.0/100,000 (95%UI 242.9–306.4).

evidence: The claim is supported by incidence rate data analysis.

claim: High systolic blood pressure ranks first in global prevalence among all conditions analyzed.

claim: High body mass index ranks second in global prevalence among all conditions analyzed.
source: The comorbid conditions, high SBP and high BMI, ranks first and second followed by CKD and T2D, and interestingly all rank above stroke.

claim: Type 1 diabetes age-standardized prevalence rates overtook intracerebral hemorrhage in the last decade.
source: We also observe that though there is a continuous increase in prevalence rates in the last decade, the ranking of stroke or its comorbid conditions does not change over the years, with the exception of T1D ASPRs overtaking ICH.
evidence: The claim is supported by prevalence rate trend analysis.

claim: Africa has an age-standardized mortality rate for high systolic blood pressure of 206.2/100,000 (95%UI 177.4–234.2) in 2019.

evidence: The claim is supported by regional mortality rate data and population data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Middle East has an age-standardized mortality rate for high systolic blood pressure of 198.6/100,000 (95%UI 162.8–234.4) in 2019.

claim: Strokes group has the highest proportional mortality (37.1–47.2%) across all years and regions, except Oceania and America.

evidence: The claim is supported by proportional mortality analysis shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: In Oceania and America, metabolic disorders have the highest proportional mortality (39.1–42.2%) which is significantly higher compared to global proportion.

source: The age-standardized prevalence of stroke in 2019 ranges from lowest in Central and South Asia (858.5/100,000, 95%UI 737.6–979.4) to highest in East Asia (1513.1/100,000, 95%UI 1390.7–1635.5), in contrast to mortality rates, lowest in America (40.3/100,000, 95%UI 36.2–43.1) and highest in East Asia (127.7/100,000, 95%UI 104.9–150.5).
evidence: The claim is supported by regional mortality rate data analysis.

claim: Stroke ranks sixth in prevalence across all ethnogeographic locations.
source: In terms of ranking, stroke ranks sixth in prevalence across all ethnogeographic locations, but ranks second in mortality in East Asia and third in Central and South Asia and Africa.
evidence: The claim is supported by regional ranking analysis.

claim: Stroke ranks second in mortality in East Asia.
source: In terms of ranking, stroke ranks sixth in prevalence across all ethnogeographic locations, but ranks second in mortality in East Asia and third in Central and South Asia and Africa.
evidence: The claim is supported by regional ranking analysis.

claim: Stroke ranks third in mortality in Central and South Asia and Africa.
source: In terms of ranking, stroke ranks sixth in prevalence across all ethnogeographic locations, but ranks second in mortality in East Asia and third in Central and South Asia and Africa.
evidence: The claim is supported by regional ranking analysis.

claim: Diabetes is a comorbid condition for stroke but not for subarachnoid hemorrhage, and this risk is ethnic-specific.
source: Diabetes is a comorbid condition for stroke but not for SAH, and this risk is ethnic-specific (Lindgren et al., 2013; Koshy et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim cites two studies (Lindgren et al., 2013; Koshy et al., 2010) supporting the ethnic-specific nature of diabetes as a comorbid condition.

claim: Reduction in life expectancy was observed in 31 of 37 high-income countries, deduced to be due to COVID-19.
source: Studies reported reduction in life expectancy in 31 of 37 high-income countries, deduced to be due to COVID-19 (Islam et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Islam et al., 2021 as the source for this observation.

claim: Genetic risk variants for diabetes, cardiovascular disease, diabetic retinopathies and nephropathies, hypertension, inflammation, and kidney diseases have been reportedly shown to have strong ethnogenetic variation.
source: Genetic risk variants for diabetes, cardiovascular disease, diabetic retinopathies and nephropathies, hypertension, inflammation, and kidney diseases have been reportedly shown to have strong ethnogenetic variation (Shoily et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Shoily et al., 2021 as the source for this observation.

claim: Stroke accounts for approximately 20% of deaths in diabetics.
source: Stroke accounts for approximately 20% of deaths in diabetics (Banerjee et al., 2012; Boehme et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim cites two studies (Banerjee et al., 2012; Boehme et al., 2017) as the source for this statistic.

claim: Diabetics and pre-diabetics, and the duration of diabetes have been reported to have increased risk of stroke, which gets aggravated in African-Americans.
source: Diabetics and pre-diabetics, and the duration of diabetes have been reported to have increased risk of stroke, which gets aggravated in African-Americans (Banerjee et al., 2012; Boehme et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim cites two studies (Banerjee et al., 2012; Boehme et al., 2017) as the source for this observation.

claim: A UK biobank cohort study on stroke suggests that genetic and lifestyle factors were independently associated with incident stroke.
source: Similar observation in a UK biobank cohort study on stroke suggests that genetic and lifestyle factors were independently associated with incident stroke, which emphasizes the benefit of entire populations adhering to a healthy lifestyle, independent of genetic risk (Rutten-Jacobs et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Rutten-Jacobs et al., 2018 as the source for this observation.

claim: Genetic variations demonstrate inter-ethnic differences in LDL levels resulting in differential impact on dyslipidemia.
source: Genetic variations demonstrate inter-ethnic differences in LDL levels resulting in differential impact on dyslipidemia (Klarin et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Klarin et al., 2018 as the source for this observation.

claim: A meta-analysis on European, East Asian, and African-American ethnicities revealed that common variants of CDH13 and ADIPOQ regulate adiponectin levels.
source: A meta-analysis on European, East Asian, and African-American ethnicities revealed that common variants of CDH13 and ADIPOQ regulate adiponectin levels, an important component of BMI indicator (Dastani et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim cites Dastani et al., 2012 as the source for this finding.

claim: ALDH2*504Lys allele has been reported to be associated with high BMI, increased tolerance of alcohol, high SBP, and decreased high-density lipoprotein in East Asians.
source: ALDH2*504Lys allele has been reported to be associated with high BMI, increased tolerance of alcohol, high SBP, and decreased high-density lipoprotein in East Asians (Takeuchi et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim cites two studies (Takeuchi et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2010) as the source for this association.

claim: MEGASTROKE consortium reported five variants associated with blood pressure and two with LDL cholesterol.
source: MEGASTROKE consortium on stroke and its comorbid factors reported five variants associated with blood pressure, two with LDL cholesterol and reported that all stroke subtypes were associated with a Genetic Risk Score for high SBP (Malik et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Malik et al., 2018 as the source for this finding.

claim: MEGASTROKE consortium reported that all stroke subtypes were associated with a Genetic Risk Score for high systolic blood pressure.
source: MEGASTROKE consortium on stroke and its comorbid factors reported five variants associated with blood pressure, two with LDL cholesterol and reported that all stroke subtypes were associated with a Genetic Risk Score for high SBP (Malik et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim cites Malik et al., 2018 as the source for this finding.

claim: A study on ischemic heart disease and type 2 diabetes in European populations reported Polygenic risk score with similar accuracy across Europeans, to a lesser extent to South and East Asian populations, and very poor transferability for Africans.
source: A study on IHD, T2D in European populations with different healthcare systems, and local population substructures reported Polygenic risk score with similar accuracy across Europeans, to a lesser extent to South and East Asian populations, and very poor transferability for Africans (Mars et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim cites Mars et al., 2022 as the source for this finding.

claim: COL4A1 and COL4A2 were common denominators for most of the stroke subtypes.
source: While COL4A1 and COL4A2 were common denominators for most of the stroke subtypes, high-density lipoprotein was inversely associated with small vessel stroke (Meschia, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Meschia, 2020 as the source for this observation.

claim: High-density lipoprotein was inversely associated with small vessel stroke.
source: While COL4A1 and COL4A2 were common denominators for most of the stroke subtypes, high-density lipoprotein was inversely associated with small vessel stroke (Meschia, 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Meschia, 2020 as the source for this observation.

claim: The INTERSTROKE study reported that high systolic blood pressure was significantly associated with intracerebral hemorrhage.
source: The INTERSTROKE study on stroke subtypes reported that among comorbid factors, high SBP was significantly associated with ICH and diabetes, cardiac issues, and apolipoproteins with ischemic stroke (O'Donnell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim cites O'Donnell et al., 2016 as the source for this finding.

claim: The INTERSTROKE study reported that diabetes, cardiac issues, and apolipoproteins were significantly associated with ischemic stroke.
source: The INTERSTROKE study on stroke subtypes reported that among comorbid factors, high SBP was significantly associated with ICH and diabetes, cardiac issues, and apolipoproteins with ischemic stroke (O'Donnell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim cites O'Donnell et al., 2016 as the source for this finding.

claim: Ischemic stroke associated with ApoB/ApoA1 ratio had higher population attributable fraction (67.6%) in Southeast Asia compared to Western Europe, North America, and Australia (24.8%).
source: Ischemic stroke associated with ApoB/ApoA1 ratio had higher (67.6%) population attributable fraction (PAF) in Southeast Asia compared to Western Europe, North America, and Australia (24.8%), while ischemic stroke associated with atrial fibrillation had lower PAF in South Asia (3.1%) compared to the rest (17.1%) (O'Donnell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim cites O'Donnell et al., 2016 as the source for this finding.

claim: Ischemic stroke associated with atrial fibrillation had lower population attributable fraction in South Asia (3.1%) compared to the rest (17.1%).
source: Ischemic stroke associated with ApoB/ApoA1 ratio had higher (67.6%) population attributable fraction (PAF) in Southeast Asia compared to Western Europe, North America, and Australia (24.8%), while ischemic stroke associated with atrial fibrillation had lower PAF in South Asia (3.1%) compared to the rest (17.1%) (O'Donnell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim cites O'Donnell et al., 2016 as the source for this finding.

claim: Novel ethnic-specific genetic variants such as SUMOylation pathway in Indians have been identified for stroke.
source: Emerging studies like novel ethnic-specific genetic variants, such as SUMOylation pathway in Indians (Kumar et al., 2021), SFXN4 and TMEM108 in Africans (Keene et al., 2020) indicate the involvement of different pathways among different ethnicities in stroke.
evidence: The claim cites Kumar et al., 2021 as the source for this finding.

claim: Novel ethnic-specific genetic variants SFXN4 and TMEM108 in Africans have been identified for stroke.
source: Emerging studies like novel ethnic-specific genetic variants, such as SUMOylation pathway in Indians (Kumar et al., 2021), SFXN4 and TMEM108 in Africans (Keene et al., 2020) indicate the involvement of different pathways among different ethnicities in stroke.
evidence: The claim cites Keene et al., 2020 as the source for this finding.

claim: The A allele of c.*84G>A loci in CETP gene was found to be a risk factor for ischemic heart disease in South Asians.
source: The A allele of c.*84G>A loci in CETP gene was found to be a risk factor for IHD in South Asians (Ganesan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim cites Ganesan et al., 2016 as the source for this finding.

claim: High systolic blood pressure was found to be a risk factor in all major stroke subtypes except lobar intracerebral hemorrhage.
source: High SBP was found to be a risk factor in all major stroke subtypes except lobar ICH (Georgakis et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites Georgakis et al., 2020 as the source for this finding.

claim: The risk variants rs528002287 (locus 15q26.3) in PCSK6 and rs148010464 (locus 1q31.1) an intergenic variant in PLA2G4A/LINC01036 for stroke were found to be associated with cardioembolic stroke and small vessel stroke in South Asians.
source: The risk variants rs528002287 (locus 15q26.3) in PCSK6 and rs148010464 (locus 1q31.1) an intergenic variant in PLA2G4A/LINC01036 for stroke were unique to South Asia, and were found to be associated with cardioembolic stroke and small vessel stroke in South Asians (Kumar et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites Kumar et al., 2021 as the source for this finding.

claim: A recent INTERSTROKE study reported the association of short sleep duration with increased risk for stroke to be highest in the South Asian ethnicity (Odds Ratio 9.13, 95% Confidence Interval 5.86–14.66).
source: A recent INTERSTROKE study reported the association of short sleep duration with increased risk for stroke to be highest in the South Asian ethnicity (Odds Ratio 9.13, 95% Confidence Interval 5.86–14.66) (Mc Carthy et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim cites Mc Carthy et al., 2023 as the source for this finding.

claim: Decreased sleep quantity and quality have been reported to increase blood pressure.
source: Decreased sleep quantity and quality have been reported to increase blood pressure (Sabanayagam and Shankar, 2010), prevalence for which was found to be highest for South Asians in our study.
evidence: The claim cites Sabanayagam and Shankar, 2010 as the source for this observation.

claim: PCSK6 is known to regulate sodium homeostasis and thereby maintain diastolic blood pressure.
source: These observations are interesting as PCSK6 is known to regulate sodium homeostasis and thereby maintain diastolic blood pressure (Li et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim cites two studies (Li et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2015) as the source for this knowledge.

claim: Reports indicate 2.34-fold difference in the expression of PCSK6 during maintenance phase of hypertension.
source: Reports also indicate 2.34-fold difference in the expression of PCSK6 during maintenance phase of hypertension (Marques et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim cites Marques et al., 2010 as the source for this observation.

claim: PCSK6 has been reported to be involved in processing of precursors of Melanin Concentrating hormone (MCH) under certain conditions.
source: PCSK6 has also been reported to be involved in processing of precursors of Melanin Concentrating hormone (MCH) under certain conditions (Viale et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim cites Viale et al., 1999 as the source for this observation.

claim: Melanin Concentrating hormone is known to play a central role in promoting and stabilizing sleep.
source: MCH is known to play a central role in promoting and stabilizing sleep (Jego et al., 2013; Konadhode et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim cites two studies (Jego et al., 2013; Konadhode et al., 2013) as the source for this knowledge.

claim: In insomnia patients, PLA2G4A was reported to be upregulated by 1.88-fold after improvement in sleep.
source: In insomnia patients, PLA2G4A was reported to be upregulated by 1.88-fold after improvement in sleep (Livingston et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim cites Livingston et al., 2015 as the source for this observation.

claim: In sleep deprived mice, expression of PLA2G4A was downregulated.
source: In sleep deprived mice, glycolytic pathway and lipid metabolism were upregulated and expression of PLA2G4A was downregulated (Hinard et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim cites Hinard et al., 2012 as the source for this observation.

claim: PLA2G4A is known to play a role in the metabolism of phospholipids, production of lipid mediators, and the release of arachidonic acid.
source: These observations are interesting as PLA2G4A is known to play a role in the metabolism of phospholipids, production of lipid mediators, and the release of arachidonic acid (Burke and Dennis, 2009; Shimizu et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim cites two studies (Burke and Dennis, 2009; Shimizu et al., 2006) as the source for this knowledge.

claim: Arachidonic acid is involved in signaling pathways of metabolic processes like release of insulin and glucose disposal.
source: Arachidonic acid is involved in signaling pathways of metabolic processes like release of insulin and glucose disposal (Chen et al., 1996; Nugent et al., 2001; Wolford et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim cites three studies (Chen et al., 1996; Nugent et al., 2001; Wolford et al., 2003) as the source for this knowledge.

claim: PLA2G4A plays a role in the production of pro-thrombotic TXA2 and inhibition of PLA2G4A can reduce platelet aggregation and thromboembolism.
source: PLA2G4A also plays a role in the production of pro-thrombotic TXA2 and thus, inhibition of PLA2G4A can reduce platelet aggregation and thromboembolism (Murakami et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim cites Murakami et al., 2011 as the source for this knowledge.

claim: Most variations in the human genome are rare and unique to specific subpopulations.
source: One of the major conclusions from the 1000 Genomes Project was that most variations in the human genome are rare and unique to specific subpopulations (Abecasis et al., 2010; Abecasis et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim cites two studies (Abecasis et al., 2010; Abecasis et al., 2012) as the source for this conclusion.

claim: Genes like ABCA1, PCSK9, and LDLR carry both common variants with moderate effects as well as rare variants with large effect for lipid levels.
source: Examples of genes like ABCA1, PCSK9, and LDLR (Kathiresan et al., 2009; Lusis and Pajukanta, 2008), which carries both common variants with moderate effects as well as rare variants with large effect for lipid levels indicate that genes can contain both types of variants associated with a complex trait.
evidence: The claim cites two studies (Kathiresan et al., 2009; Lusis and Pajukanta, 2008) as the source for these examples.

claim: The comorbid conditions that act as risk drivers for stroke differed by regions, with more of metabolic risk in America and Europe, in contrast to high systolic blood pressure in Asian and African regions.
source: Interestingly, the comorbid conditions that act as risk drivers for stroke differed by regions, with more of metabolic risk in America and Europe, in contrast to high systolic blood pressure in Asian and African regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of regional differences in comorbid conditions presented in the manuscript.

claim: GWAS risk loci of stroke and its comorbid conditions indicate distinct population stratification for each of these conditions, signifying population-specific risk.
source: GWAS risk loci of stroke and its comorbid conditions indicate distinct population stratification for each of these conditions, signifying for population-specific risk.
evidence: The claim is supported by the population structure analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Unique ethnic-specific risk variants and their distinct patterns of linkage disequilibrium uncover the drivers for phenotypic variation.
source: Unique ethnic-specific risk variants and their distinct patterns of linkage disequilibrium further uncover the drivers for phenotypic variation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the LD analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The different socio-economic regions are driven by different risk factors of stroke.
source: The different socio-economic regions are driven by different risk factors of stroke and low-frequency variants could be playing a role in the differences in burden of stroke seen in the different regions as shown in Figure 9.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Low-frequency variants could be playing a role in the differences in burden of stroke seen in different regions.
source: The different socio-economic regions are driven by different risk factors of stroke and low-frequency variants could be playing a role in the differences in burden of stroke seen in the different regions as shown in Figure 9.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 9.
